### Fitting tables

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal" title="Nerdy details"}

#### Model predictions

For each test $t$, the data provides the joint distribution $J_t(i, j)$ of the provisional advice and test result, as shown in @eq-joint.
The model predicts the same share $q_t(i, j)$ (the model's counterpart of $J_t(i, j)$),
which is the probability that the pupil's evaluations are within the rectangular area defined by the thresholds of $i$ and $j$ (see @eq-thresholds):

- the provisional advice thresholds $\lambda_i$ and $\lambda_{i+1}$, and
- the test result thresholds $\tau_j$ and $\tau_{j+1}$.

To obtain $q_t(i, j)$, we need to standardize the thresholds, i.e., its boundaries, to the latent scale of the provisional advice $L^*$, which is the reference indicator in our measurement model.
We do this by subtracting the evaluation's mean and dividing by its standard deviation from Equations [-@eq-reduced-model] and [-@eq-reduced-variance-correlation]:

$$
u_{t, i} = \frac{\lambda_i - \mu_t}{\sigma_t}, \quad
v_{t, j} = \frac{\tau_j - (a_t + b_t \mu_t)}{s_t}.
$$ {#eq-standardized-thresholds}

The standardized thresholds $u_{t, i}$ and $v_{t, j}$ are the boundaries of the rectangular area in the bivariate normal distribution of the reduced model.
Then, $q_t(i, j)$ is the probability mass within this area, which can be computed using the bivariate normal cumulative distribution function $\Phi_2$ [@olsson1979]:

$$
q_t(i, j) =
\Phi_2(u_{t, i+1}, v_{t, j+1}, \rho_t) -
\Phi_2(u_{t, i}, v_{t, j+1}, \rho_t) -
\Phi_2(u_{t, i+1}, v_{t, j}, \rho_t) +
\Phi_2(u_{t, i}, v_{t, j}, \rho_t),
$$ {#eq-model-probability}

i.e., the probability below the upper-right corner,
minus the areas to the left and below,
plus the lower-left corner that was subtracted twice.

CvTE provides $J_t(i, j)$ as the share of pupils with provisional advice $i$ and test result $j$ in test $t$.
To approximate the number of pupils with these evaluations,
we multiply the share by the number of pupils in test $t$ and the fraction of pupils in year $y$, for whom the provisional advice is available [@cvte2025; @cvte2026]:

$$
n_t(i, j) = N_t f_y J_t(i, j).
$$ {#eq-model-counts}

The resulting pseudo counts are shown in @fig-model-counts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-model-counts
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-cap: "Pseudo model counts of pupils per provisional advice $i$ and test result $j$, by test and year (choose a test and a year above the plot).  Each bubble represents the pseudo count for that combination. Cells under 0.05% are not shown."  # nolint: line_length_linter
model_counts_plot(model_counts, gap_matrix)
```

#### Likelihood

As mentioned in @sec-measurement-model, the model assumes that pupils are independent.
Then the counts $n_t(i, j)$ follow a multinomial distribution with probabilities $q_t(i, j)$.
The log-likelihood of the model is then given by:

$$
\log \mathcal{L} = \sum_t \sum_{i, j} n_t(i, j) \log q_t(i, j).
$$ {#eq-log-likelihood}

We fit all tests of a year jointly, so they share the thresholds $\lambda$ and $\tau$: one common ruler.
Separate thresholds for each test could absorb differences in leniency.
We can maximize the log-likelihood to find the best-fitting parameters of the published data.
The model is constrained: each $10 \times 6$ table has 59 free cell probabilities, compared with five parameters per non-reference test and 14 thresholds shared across tests.
The pseudo counts use rounded percentages and only pupils with known provisional advice; pupils are also clustered in schools.
Naive multinomial standard errors would ignore these features, so we assess fit descriptively.

As mentioned in @sec-measurement-model,
the measurement scale is set by the teacher's advice ($\mu_\text{ref} = 0$ and $\sigma^2_\text{ref} = 1$);
the origin of the test's scale is set by the test's leniency ($\beta_\text{ref} = 0$).
We cannot set the test's sensitivity $\alpha_\text{ref}$ to a fixed value, because it is not identifiable.
Instead, we set $\psi^2_\text{ref} = 1$, which fixes the test units without changing fitted probabilities.
The value of $\alpha_\text{ref}$ depends on the teacher/test error split, identified in the next step.

#### Parameters

There are two types of restrictions on the parameters:
thresholds must increase ($\lambda_1 < \dots < \lambda_9$, $\tau_1 < \dots < \tau_5$), and
spreads must be positive ($\sigma_t, \psi_t > 0$).
We handle these restrictions by transforming these parameters to unconstrained parameters as follows:

- the first threshold of each scale is estimated directly -- this sets the origin of the scale,
- the gaps between consecutive thresholds are estimated on the log scale,
i.e., $\lambda_{l+1} - \lambda_l = e^{\gamma_l}$ and $\tau_{l+1} - \tau_l = e^{\zeta_l}$, --
this ensures that the thresholds increase by forcing the gaps to be positive,
- the spreads are estimated on the log scale, i.e., $\sigma_t = e^{\eta_t}$ and $\psi_t = e^{\xi_t}$. --
this ensures that the spreads are positive.

The final set of parameters to be estimated is then:

- the first threshold of the teacher's advice $\lambda_1$ ($\#$ = 1),
- the gaps between consecutive thresholds of the teacher's advice $\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_8$ ($\#$ = 8),
- the first threshold of the test result $\tau_1$ ($\#$ = 1),
- the gaps between consecutive thresholds of the test result $\zeta_1, \dots, \zeta_4$ ($\#$ = 4),
- the slope of the reference test $b_\text{ref}$ ($\#$ = 1),
- the parameters of the other tests $(\mu_t, \log \sigma_t, a_t, b_t, \log \psi_t)$ ($\#$ = 5 per test).

We estimate per-test parameters for the tests in each year, with only its slope free for the reference test; its other parameters are fixed by the normalization.
Then, the total number of parameters is
`{r} length(fits[["2025"]]$par)` in 2025 (`{r} length(fits[["2025"]]$counts)` tests) and
`{r} length(fits[["2026"]]$par)` in 2026 (`{r} length(fits[["2026"]]$counts)` tests).

We maximize the log-likelihood in @eq-log-likelihood with the quasi-Newton L-BFGS-B algorithm [@byrd1995],
a quasi-Newton method that uses the slope and an estimate of the curvature to choose each step.
We then use a dissimilarity index to summarize the fit (@fig-dissimilarity-index), which is the share of pupils that
would have to move to another cell for the fitted table to equal the published one:

$$
\text{DI}_t = \frac12 \sum_{i, j} \left| \hat q_t(i, j) - J_t(i, j) \right|.
$$ {#eq-dissimilarity-index}

```{r}
#| label: fig-dissimilarity-index
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Dissimilarity index of the model fit per test and year. The index represents the share of pupils that would have to move to another cell. Open circle: 2025, filled: 2026."  # nolint: line_length_linter
dissimilarity_plot(fit_quality)
```

The dissimilarity index is about 3–6% for Lib, IEP, and Dia, compared with 7–13% for AMN, ROUTE 8, and DOE.
The latter tests have more pupils with PrO advice in the published tables; this population difference may contribute to the weaker fit, but the index does not establish its cause.

```{r}
knitr::kable(fit_quality, digits = 3)
```
